PROP
41
PROHIBITS NEW STATE TAXES THAT EXCLUDE REVENUES FROM STATE SPENDING LIMIT. REQUIRES AUDITS FOR NEW STATE SPECIAL TAXES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Nullifies state taxes enacted after January 1, 2026 that exempt their revenues from voter-approved state spending limit. Requires pre-election and recurring audits of programs funded by new special taxes. Fiscal Impact: The net fiscal effect is unknown as it depends on future decisions by voters, the Legislature, and other policymakers. Supporters: CA Society of Certified Public Accountants (CalCPAs); CalAsian Chamber of Commerce; California Taxpayers Association (CalTax) Opponents: US Senator Bernie Sanders; SEIU United Healthcare Workers West
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: When special taxes are proposed by voter initiatives, the California State Auditor would review programs funded by the tax before the initiative appears on the ballot. The California State Auditor also would regularly review programs funded by special taxes approved by voters or the Legislature. In addition, the state might not be able to exclude any new special tax spending from its spending limit.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: The California State Auditor’s responsibility to review government programs would not change. The state spending limit requirements would not change.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
Californians deserve better results for our taxes. Billions have flowed into programs like homelessness, with too little to show for it. Prop. 41 requires the independent State Auditor to conduct PUBLIC AUDITS of programs funded by new taxes—so we get more transparency, more accountability and better outcomes for taxpayers.
CON
Prop. 41 isn’t really about audits—it’s a billionaire-funded trick designed to undo the California Billionaire Tax. Billionaires would rather millions of Californians lose healthcare than pay a modest tax on their extreme wealth. Don’t fall for the billionaires’ lies. Vote NO on 41.

California citizens may propose state laws and constitutional amendments through the statewide initiative process.
Supporters of an initiative collect signatures from registered voters to qualify their initiative for the ballot.
State law sets how many valid signatures supporters must collect to qualify their initiative for the ballot.
...
PROPOSAL
Requires One-Time Audits Before Special Taxes Appear on the Ballot Through the Voter Initiative Process.
Proposition 41 requires the State Auditor to review each program that would receive funds from a new or increased special tax proposed through the voter initiative process.
This audit would occur after supporters collect 25 percent of the signatures needed to qualify a measure for the ballot, which is before it is known whether the initiative will qualify for the ballot.
Proposition 41 specifies what the State Auditor would include in these audits, including identifying ways to reduce an audited program's annual costs by 10 percent.
Proposition 41 requires the State Auditor to write a summary of each audit.
If a proposed voter initiative with a special tax qualifies for the ballot, Proposition 41 requires the State Auditor's summary to be included in the VIG.
If voters approve the special tax, the cost of the one-time audit would be paid from the new tax revenues.

6. EDITORIAL: We asked the No on Prop. 41 campaign why voters should reject the measure
https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-41-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/
Californians are being asked to vote "yes" or "no" on 14 ballot measures.
One of them is Proposition 41, which, according to the Legislative Analyst's Office, would require an audit on new or increased special taxes before they appear on the ballot and ongoing audits of programs that receive funding from special taxes.
Special taxes may also be subjected to spending limits.
Voting "yes" would mean that the state auditor reviews programs funded by special taxes before they're on the ballot and on an ongoing basis while opening the possibility that spending limits are attached to the special taxes.
Because of the requirements it imposes on new special taxes, voting "yes" could also mean that Proposition 40 (the "billionaire tax"), even if it gets enough votes, is stopped from becoming law if the courts determine that it conflicts with Prop.
41.
Voting "no" would mean that the state auditor's role in reviewing government programs stays the same, as would spending limit requirements.
Supporters of the measure, also known as the Prohibit Excluding New State Taxes from Spending Limit and Require Special Tax Audits Initiative, favor the increased transparency, oversight and analysis regarding special taxes.

PROP
41
PROHIBITS NEW STATE TAXES THAT EXCLUDE REVENUES FROM STATE SPENDING LIMIT. REQUIRES AUDITS FOR NEW STATE SPECIAL TAXES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Nullifies state taxes enacted after January 1, 2026 that exempt their revenues from voter-approved state spending limit. Requires pre-election and recurring audits of programs funded by new special taxes. Fiscal Impact: The net fiscal effect is unknown as it depends on future decisions by voters, the Legislature, and other policymakers. Supporters: CA Society of Certified Public Accountants (CalCPAs); CalAsian Chamber of Commerce; California Taxpayers Association (CalTax) Opponents: US Senator Bernie Sanders; SEIU United Healthcare Workers West
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: When special taxes are proposed by voter initiatives, the California State Auditor would review programs funded by the tax before the initiative appears on the ballot. The California State Auditor also would regularly review programs funded by special taxes approved by voters or the Legislature. In addition, the state might not be able to exclude any new special tax spending from its spending limit.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: The California State Auditor’s responsibility to review government programs would not change. The state spending limit requirements would not change.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
Californians deserve better results for our taxes. Billions have flowed into programs like homelessness, with too little to show for it. Prop. 41 requires the independent State Auditor to conduct PUBLIC AUDITS of programs funded by new taxes—so we get more transparency, more accountability and better outcomes for taxpayers.
CON
Prop. 41 isn’t really about audits—it’s a billionaire-funded trick designed to undo the California Billionaire Tax. Billionaires would rather millions of Californians lose healthcare than pay a modest tax on their extreme wealth. Don’t fall for the billionaires’ lies. Vote NO on 41.

PROP
41
PROHIBITS NEW STATE TAXES THAT EXCLUDE REVENUES FROM STATE SPENDING LIMIT. REQUIRES AUDITS FOR NEW STATE SPECIAL TAXES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Nullifies state taxes enacted after January 1, 2026 that exempt their revenues from voter-approved state spending limit. Requires pre-election and recurring audits of programs funded by new special taxes. Fiscal Impact: The net fiscal effect is unknown as it depends on future decisions by voters, the Legislature, and other policymakers. Supporters: CA Society of Certified Public Accountants (CalCPAs); CalAsian Chamber of Commerce; California Taxpayers Association (CalTax) Opponents: US Senator Bernie Sanders; SEIU United Healthcare Workers West
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: When special taxes are proposed by voter initiatives, the California State Auditor would review programs funded by the tax before the initiative appears on the ballot. The California State Auditor also would regularly review programs funded by special taxes approved by voters or the Legislature. In addition, the state might not be able to exclude any new special tax spending from its spending limit.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: The California State Auditor’s responsibility to review government programs would not change. The state spending limit requirements would not change.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
Californians deserve better results for our taxes. Billions have flowed into programs like homelessness, with too little to show for it. Prop. 41 requires the independent State Auditor to conduct PUBLIC AUDITS of programs funded by new taxes—so we get more transparency, more accountability and better outcomes for taxpayers.
CON
Prop. 41 isn’t really about audits—it’s a billionaire-funded trick designed to undo the California Billionaire Tax. Billionaires would rather millions of Californians lose healthcare than pay a modest tax on their extreme wealth. Don’t fall for the billionaires’ lies. Vote NO on 41.

How this is built
Proposition 41 is forecast as a other taxes measure whose Yes vote leans Republican . Comparable measures from 2018 to 2024 set how far its Yes share moves with California 's partisanship, and each county moves with its own age, education, race and density mix as well as its 2024 presidential vote, so no two counties share a margin by default. How it reached the ballot moves it further. Polls then pull the forecast toward them by recency and size, after splitting undecided voters two to one for No. Sources: elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/ccrov/2026/june/26179jj.pdf), growsf.org (https://growsf.org/news/2026-07-02-14-state-measures/), ppic.org (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), escholarship.org (https://escholarship.org/content/qt3w14s99c/qt3w14s99c.pdf). How this is built
Proposition 41 is forecast as a other taxes measure whose Yes vote leans Republican . Comparable measures from 2018 to 2024 set how far its Yes share moves with California 's partisanship, and each county moves with its own age, education, race and density mix as well as its 2024 presidential vote, so no two counties share a margin by default. How it reached the ballot moves it further. Also, undecideds in IGS broke toward No. Also, note that in a midterm with lower turnout and higher-propensity older/Republican voters, tax-limit measures can overperform polls. But the polls are of likely voters.

One consideration: the "no" side benefits from the framing that it's a billionaire-funded trick. Also, the LA Times/IGS poll shows Prop 41 at 38-47, quite a bit behind.

Also, one more consideration: whether Prop 41 passing actually matters — but the question just asks which side is more likely to win, i.e., Yes or No.

Additional angle: There might be an interaction — if Prop 40 fails, the messaging for Prop 41 could be different. But polls are polls.

Weighing: PPIC 48-49 (No +1), IGS 38-47 (No +9), SurveyUSA? Let me check whether SurveyUSA polled Prop 41. The electcademocrats page listed SurveyUSA for Prop 39 (49-42) and Prop 40 (44-43) but not Prop 41 apparently. So there are just two late polls.

Forecast: No 79.6%. I'll go with "no".

Let me do one final check for any very last-minute polls (Nov 1-2) or news that changed things, e.g., a court ruling on Prop 41 or an endorsement shift.

However, I should consider a counterargument: the Yes side has a massive funding advantage, and Prop 42 (similar) is polling ahead at 51%. Also, undecideds in IGS broke toward No. Also, note that in a midterm with lower turnout and higher-propensity older/Republican voters, tax-limit measures can overperform polls. But the polls are of likely voters.

One consideration: the "no" side benefits from the framing that it's a billionaire-funded trick. Also, the LA Times/IGS poll shows Prop 41 at 38-47, quite a bit behind.

Also, one more consideration: whether Prop 41 passing actually matters — but the question just asks which side is more likely to win, i.e., Yes or No.

Additional angle: There might be an interaction — if Prop 40 fails, the messaging for Prop 41 could be different. But polls are polls.

Weighing: PPIC 48-49 (No +1), IGS 38-47 (No +9), SurveyUSA? Let me check whether SurveyUSA polled Prop 41. The electcademocrats page listed SurveyUSA for Prop 39 (49-42) and Prop 40 (44-43) but not Prop 41 apparently. So there are just two late polls.

Forecast: No 79.6%. I'll go with "no".

Let me do one final check for any very last-minute polls (Nov 1-2) or news that changed things, e.g., a court ruling on Prop 41 or an endorsement shift.

Confirmation: as of November 2, 2026, no newer polls. Prop 41: IGS 38-47 (16 undecided), PPIC 48-49. Both trailing. Forecast: No 79.6%.

Additional consideration: In California, initiative measures with high undecided typically break toward "no" — historically, undecided voters on ballot measures tend to break against. And in IGS, undecideds broke strongly against Prop 41 from September to October (no went 33→47 while yes held at 37-38). That's a strong signal.

Also, the anti-billionaire sentiment: the "No" campaign framing that Prop 41 is a billionaire-funded trick. Even though Prop 40 itself is failing, Prop 41 is seen as a deceptive billionaire measure, so the coalition against is broader (Bernie Sanders, SEIU, Democrats — Democrats oppose 56-38).

Also note turnout: midterm electorate is more Democratic-leaning in California (Becerra leading 61-37 per PPIC), which is bad for Prop 41 (Yes side leans Republican).

So the "No" side is more likely to win. The question format: "Which side is more likely to win? Answer with only yes or no." This means: is the Yes side more likely to win? Answer: no.

Hmm, but there's ambiguity — the answer "no" could be interpreted as "the No side." Either way, "no" is the answer.

Let me do one final sanity check on whether there's any late-breaking development (e.g., a major endorsement for Yes on 41 like Newsom — note Newsom endorsed Prop 42 but not 41). Also check whether the LA Times editorial board or others endorsed. Quick search.

California Gov. Gavin Newsom pauses while discussing environmental issues in San Francisco on Sept. 29, 2026.

SACRAMENTO — Gavin Newsom’s campaign team on Friday released an almost complete list of the governor’s positions on the ballot measures California voters will decide (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/california-ballot-measures-propositions-22507044.php) in the Nov. 3 midterm election.
Opinion: This is the worst measure on California’s ballot — and Gavin Newsom supports it (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/emilyhoeven/article/prop-38-california-newsom-22495203.php)

Newsom says he will vote no on four measures:

Proposition 43: a measure that would make it harder for local governments to pass new taxes by raising the approval threshold for some new local taxes from majority to two-thirds
Proposition 44: a measure to require nonprofit federally qualified health centers to spend at least 90% of their revenue on program services that advance their charitable mission
Proposition 39: Newsom previously announced his opposition to this measure, which would impose new voter ID requirements for Californians
Proposition 40: Newsom has already appeared in ads against this measure, which would impose a new wealth tax on billionaire residents
He plans to vote for eight measures:
Proposition 1: a measure to let California borrow $11.25 billion for housing, with $10 billion for affordable rental housing and homeownership programs and $1.25 billion for veteran farm, home and mobile home purchase assistance
Proposition 2: a constitutional amendment to increase the amount of money California saves in budget reserves
Proposition 3: a measure to make permanent California’s existing higher income tax rates on high earners, which are otherwise scheduled to expire after 2030
Proposition 4: a measure that would allow state and local governments to create public financing programs for candidates who meet eligibility rules and spending limits, while barring use of those funds for legal defense fees, fines or personal campaign loans
Proposition 5: a measure inspired in part by the effort to recall Newsom in 2021 that would make statewide recalls in California simple yes or no contests for or against the removal of a politician and end the practice of voters also choosing a successor in the same election
Proposition 37: a measure to authorize up to $25 billion in bonds to fund loans for middle-income buyers of new homes
Proposition 38: a measure to authorize $8.4 billion in state general obligation bonds for immunology and immunotherapy research, split between a University of California-affiliated nonprofit institute and a grant program for public or nonprofit research institutions
Proposition 42: one of two measures designed to invalidate Proposition 40, the billionaire tax, this constitutional amendment would prohibit new state taxes on the ownership or control of personal property
Newsom is still reviewing Propositions 41 and 45, spokesperson Izzy Gardon said, and has not yet taken a position on them. Proposition 41 is the second measure designed to invalidate the billionaire tax if it passes and would require audits for programs funded by new statewide special taxes and prohibit new state taxes that would circumvent the state spending limit. Proposition 45 would limit environmental review under the California Environmental Quality Act for many new construction projects.

Here’s how Newsom is voting on California’s propositions
By Sophia Bollag (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/sophia-bollag/) , Staff Writer Oct 9, 2026
California Gov. Gavin Newsom pauses while discussing environmental issues in San Francisco on Sept. 29, 2026.
Rich Pedroncelli/Associated Press
SACRAMENTO — Gavin Newsom’s campaign team on Friday released an almost complete list of the governor’s positions on the ballot measures California voters will decide (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/california-ballot-measures-propositions-22507044.php) in the Nov. 3 midterm election.
Opinion: This is the worst measure on California’s ballot — and Gavin Newsom supports it (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/emilyhoeven/article/prop-38-california-newsom-22495203.php)
Chronicle endorsements: Editorial board’s recommendations for 2026 election (https://www.sfchronicle.com/projects/2026/california-sf-election-endorsements/)
Newsom says he will vote no on four measures:

Proposition 43: a measure that would make it harder for local governments to pass new taxes by raising the approval threshold for some new local taxes from majority to two-thirds
Proposition 44: a measure to require nonprofit federally qualified health centers to spend at least 90% of their revenue on program services that advance their charitable mission
Proposition 39: Newsom previously announced his opposition to this measure, which would impose new voter ID requirements for Californians
Proposition 40: Newsom has already appeared in ads against this measure, which would impose a new wealth tax on billionaire residents
He plans to vote for eight measures:
Proposition 1: a measure to let California borrow $11.25 billion for housing, with $10 billion for affordable rental housing and homeownership programs and $1.25 billion for veteran farm, home and mobile home purchase assistance
Proposition 2: a constitutional amendment to increase the amount of money California saves in budget reserves
Proposition 3: a measure to make permanent California’s existing higher income tax rates on high earners, which are otherwise scheduled to expire after 2030
Proposition 4: a measure that would allow state and local governments to create public financing programs for candidates who meet eligibility rules and spending limits, while barring use of those funds for legal defense fees, fines or personal campaign loans
Proposition 5: a measure inspired in part by the effort to recall Newsom in 2021 that would make statewide recalls in California simple yes or no contests for or against the removal of a politician and end the practice of voters also choosing a successor in the same election
Proposition 37: a measure to authorize up to $25 billion in bonds to fund loans for middle-income buyers of new homes
Proposition 38: a measure to authorize $8.4 billion in state general obligation bonds for immunology and immunotherapy research, split between a University of California-affiliated nonprofit institute and a grant program for public or nonprofit research institutions
Proposition 42: one of two measures designed to invalidate Proposition 40, the billionaire tax, this constitutional amendment would prohibit new state taxes on the ownership or control of personal property
Newsom is still reviewing Propositions 41 and 45, spokesperson Izzy Gardon said, and has not yet taken a position on them. Proposition 41 is the second measure designed to invalidate the billionaire tax if it passes and would require audits for programs funded by new statewide special taxes and prohibit new state taxes that would circumvent the state spending limit. Proposition 45 would limit environmental review under the California Environmental Quality Act for many new construction projects.

The governor announced his positions on most of the 14 propositions on the November ballot.
Not only has Gov.
Gavin Newsom vocally opposed the proposed California billionaire tax, but he also wants to prevent the state from ever passing a wealth tax in the future.
On Friday he endorsed Proposition 42, a ballot measure that would cancel out Proposition 40, the proposed billionaire tax.
Prop.
42 would prohibit retroactive taxes like the one-time 5% tax on assets that would apply to any billionaire who lived in California on Jan. 1, 2026 if Prop.
40 passes.
But Prop.
42, funded and placed on the ballot by billionaire and Google co-founder Sergey Brin to defeat the billionaire tax, also would go further, by banning any new taxes on personal property.
That includes pensions and 401K accounts before retirees start drawing retirement income from them.
It also includes other investments, financial assets, business holdings, art collections and all other forms of personal wealth that would be affected by the billionaire tax or any future wealth tax.

Key facts: Newsom endorsed Prop 42 (yes) but took no position on Prop 41. The Democratic Party opposes both 41 and 42; Republicans support. The LA Times/IGS poll shows Prop 41 well behind (38-47). PPIC 48-49.

One thing: Newsom's yes on 42 but no position on 41 means Prop 41 lacks the Democratic elite cover that Prop 42 has — hence Prop 42 polls ahead (51%) while Prop 41 is behind (48% / 38%).

Also the massive spending advantage for Yes on 41 hasn't translated. And the trend is downward for Yes.

Historical base rates: California ballot measures polling under 50% with undecided breaking against typically fail. On Point model: 20.4% chance for Yes, 79.6% for No.

Also worth noting: The No campaign is running aggressive ads tied to the billionaire tax battle, and there's anti-billionaire sentiment in the electorate (as reflected in Prop 40's earlier lead and Prop 43's failure, etc.). Also Prop 41 is a constitutional amendment that "nullifies taxes" — a negative framing.

One countervailing factor: In a midterm with a high-propensity electorate leaning older and more conservative (Hilton vs Becerra 37-61 suggests Dem turnout dominance), Yes on Prop 41 could overperform. Also many ballot measures do overperform relative to online polls among actual voters (online polls of likely voters tend to overstate support for progressive measures sometimes). But PPIC's likely-voter sample is generally decent.

Weighing everything: No is more likely to win, with ~70-80% probability.

Answer: "no".

PROP
41
PROHIBITS NEW STATE TAXES THAT EXCLUDE REVENUES FROM STATE SPENDING LIMIT. REQUIRES AUDITS FOR NEW STATE SPECIAL TAXES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Nullifies state taxes enacted after January 1, 2026 that exempt their revenues from voter-approved state spending limit. Requires pre-election and recurring audits of programs funded by new special taxes. Fiscal Impact: The net fiscal effect is unknown as it depends on future decisions by voters, the Legislature, and other policymakers. Supporters: CA Society of Certified Public Accountants (CalCPAs); CalAsian Chamber of Commerce; California Taxpayers Association (CalTax) Opponents: US Senator Bernie Sanders; SEIU United Healthcare Workers West
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: When special taxes are proposed by voter initiatives, the California State Auditor would review programs funded by the tax before the initiative appears on the ballot. The California State Auditor also would regularly review programs funded by special taxes approved by voters or the Legislature. In addition, the state might not be able to exclude any new special tax spending from its spending limit.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: The California State Auditor’s responsibility to review government programs would not change. The state spending limit requirements would not change.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
Californians deserve better results for our taxes. Billions have flowed into programs like homelessness, with too little to show for it. Prop. 41 requires the independent State Auditor to conduct PUBLIC AUDITS of programs funded by new taxes—so we get more transparency, more accountability and better outcomes for taxpayers.
CON
Prop. 41 isn’t really about audits—it’s a billionaire-funded trick designed to undo the California Billionaire Tax. Billionaires would rather millions of Californians lose healthcare than pay a modest tax on their extreme wealth. Don’t fall for the billionaires’ lies. Vote NO on 41.

Here’s how Newsom is voting on California’s propositions
By Sophia Bollag (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/sophia-bollag/) , Staff Writer Oct 9, 2026
California Gov. Gavin Newsom pauses while discussing environmental issues in San Francisco on Sept. 29, 2026.
Rich Pedroncelli/Associated Press
SACRAMENTO — Gavin Newsom’s campaign team on Friday released an almost complete list of the governor’s positions on the ballot measures California voters will decide (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/california-ballot-measures-propositions-22507044.php) in the Nov. 3 midterm election.
Opinion: This is the worst measure on California’s ballot — and Gavin Newsom supports it (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/emilyhoeven/article/prop-38-california-newsom-22495203.php)
Chronicle endorsements: Editorial board’s recommendations for 2026 election (https://www.sfchronicle.com/projects/2026/california-sf-election-endorsements/)
Newsom says he will vote no on four measures:
Advertisement

Proposition 43: a measure that would make it harder for local governments to pass new taxes by raising the approval threshold for some new local taxes from majority to two-thirds
Proposition 44: a measure to require nonprofit federally qualified health centers to spend at least 90% of their revenue on program services that advance their charitable mission
Proposition 39: Newsom previously announced his opposition to this measure, which would impose new voter ID requirements for Californians
Proposition 40: Newsom has already appeared in ads against this measure, which would impose a new wealth tax on billionaire residents
He plans to vote for eight measures:
Proposition 1: a measure to let California borrow $11.25 billion for housing, with $10 billion for affordable rental housing and homeownership programs and $1.25 billion for veteran farm, home and mobile home purchase assistance
Proposition 2: a constitutional amendment to increase the amount of money California saves in budget reserves
Proposition 3: a measure to make permanent California’s existing higher income tax rates on high earners, which are otherwise scheduled to expire after 2030
Proposition 4: a measure that would allow state and local governments to create public financing programs for candidates who meet eligibility rules and spending limits, while barring use of those funds for legal defense fees, fines or personal campaign loans
Proposition 5: a measure inspired in part by the effort to recall Newsom in 2021 that would make statewide recalls in California simple yes or no contests for or against the removal of a politician and end the practice of voters also choosing a successor in the same election
Proposition 37: a measure to authorize up to $25 billion in bonds to fund loans for middle-income buyers of new homes
Proposition 38: a measure to authorize $8.4 billion in state general obligation bonds for immunology and immunotherapy research, split between a University of California-affiliated nonprofit institute and a grant program for public or nonprofit research institutions
Proposition 42: one of two measures designed to invalidate Proposition 40, the billionaire tax, this constitutional amendment would prohibit new state taxes on the ownership or control of personal property
Newsom is still reviewing Propositions 41 and 45, spokesperson Izzy Gardon said, and has not yet taken a position on them. Proposition 41 is the second measure designed to invalidate the billionaire tax if it passes and would require audits for programs funded by new statewide special taxes and prohibit new state taxes that would circumvent the state spending limit. Proposition 45 would limit environmental review under the California Environmental Quality Act for many new construction projects.

Key facts: Newsom endorsed Prop 42 (yes) but took no position on Prop 41. The Democratic Party opposes both 41 and 42; Republicans support. The LA Times/IGS poll shows Prop 41 well behind (38-47). PPIC 48-49.

One thing: Newsom's yes on 42 but no position on 41 means Prop 41 lacks the Democratic elite cover that Prop 42 has — hence Prop 42 polls ahead (51%) while Prop 41 is behind (48% / 38%).

Also the massive spending advantage for Yes on 41 hasn't translated. And the trend is downward for Yes.

Historical base rates: California ballot measures polling under 50% with undecided breaking against typically fail. On Point model: 20.4% chance for Yes, 79.6% for No.

Also worth noting: The No campaign is running aggressive ads tied to the billionaire tax battle, and there's anti-billionaire sentiment in the electorate (as reflected in Prop 40's earlier lead and Prop 43's failure, etc.). Also Prop 41 is a constitutional amendment that "nullifies taxes" — a negative framing.

One countervailing factor: In a midterm with a high-propensity electorate leaning older and more conservative (Hilton vs Becerra 37-61 suggests Dem turnout dominance), Yes on Prop 41 could overperform. Also many ballot measures do overperform relative to online polls among actual voters (online polls of likely voters tend to overstate support for progressive measures sometimes). But PPIC's likely-voter sample is generally decent.

Weighing everything: No is more likely to win, with ~70-80% probability.

Answer: "no".

The question: "Which side is more likely to win? ... Answer with only yes or no." The answer to "is the yes side more likely to win?" is no. And the No side is more likely to win → "no". Both interpretations converge on "no".
